1The big idea (why this chapter exists)

🧸 ELI5

You know how you can't just say you won a game — you have to actually show it? Geometry is the same. You're not allowed to say "this side equals that side" just because it looks true. You have to prove it with steps everybody agrees on.

Chapter 2 teaches you the rules of arguing with math: how to make a promise ("if this… then that…"), how to test that promise, and how to write your proof down so it's airtight like a detective's case file. 🕵️

📝 Test-speak

Inductive reasoning = noticing a pattern and making a guess (a conjecture): "every dog I've met is friendly, so probably all dogs are friendly." Good for discovering ideas — but it never proves anything.

Deductive reasoning = using facts, definitions and rules to reach a conclusion that must be true: "All dogs are animals. Rex is a dog. → Rex is an animal." Geometry proofs are 100% deductive.

Your notes' header compared these two — geometry lives on the right side.

2If → Then promises (Conditional Statements)

🧸 ELI5

A conditional statement is just a promise:

IF you clean your room, THEN you get ice cream.

The IF part is called the hypothesis (nickname: p). The THEN part is the conclusion (nickname: q). One promise, two halves: the setup and the payoff.

The conditional machine: put a true setup in, the payoff must follow.
📝 Test-speak

A conditional statement is written if p, then q — or p → q ("p implies q"). These four orderings from your notes all mean exactly the same promise:

Written as…Same promise in disguise
If p then qthe normal version
p implies qfancy word for "then"
p only if q"you get the payoff ONLY IF the setup happened"
q if pthe "if" moved to the middle — still p → q
⚠️ Trap alert

The "if" likes to hide. In class the "if" is often in the middle of the sentence — always rewrite it as If…, then… before you label anything. And watch out for "only if": whatever follows "only if" is the conclusion, even though it feels like it should be first. Sneaky!

Your class examples, labeled ✅

StatementRewritten If→Thenp (hypothesis)q (conclusion)
"If 3x − 7 = 32, then x = 13."already in form3x − 7 = 32x = 13
"I can't sleep if I'm not tired.""If I'm not tired, then I can't sleep."I'm not tiredI can't sleep
"I'll try if you will.""If you will, then I'll try."you willI'll try
"x = 5 only if x² = 25.""If x = 5, then x² = 25."x = 5x² = 25
✏️ Try it

Label hypothesis and conclusion: "If a point is the midpoint of a segment, then it divides the segment into two equal parts."

tap to reveal
p = "a point is the midpoint of a segment"  ·  q = "it divides the segment into two equal parts". (Bonus: this one works backwards too — that's coming in §5.)

3Flip it: the Converse

🧸 ELI5

The converse takes your promise and simply swaps the two halves — no "not" involved, just a trade:

If p, then q  →  If q, then p

Pizza version: "If it's a pizza, then it's food." → converse: "If it's food, then it's a pizza." 🍕 One of those is… very wrong. That's the whole point of this section: swapping can break a perfectly good promise.

📝 Test-speak

Converse: formed by exchanging the hypothesis and conclusion. Original p → q becomes q → p.

Your notes' example: "If I study well, then I can score good" → converse: "If I can score good, then I study well." (Swap h and c — your teacher labeled them with little h and c under the sentence!)

⚠️ Trap alert

A true statement does NOT guarantee a true converse.

  • "If x = 5, then x² = 25." ✅ true — but converse "If x² = 25, then x = 5" ❌ FALSE: x could be −5! (−5)² = 25 too.
  • "If it is raining, then the ground is wet." ✅ — converse "If the ground is wet, then it is raining" ❌ — maybe it's just a sprinkler. 💦

So on the test: checking a converse's truth is its own task. Don't copy the original's answer!

✏️ Try it

Write the converse: "If three points lie on the same line, then they are collinear." And… is the converse true this time?

tap to reveal

Converse: "If three points are collinear, then they lie on the same line." ✅ True both ways! (That's why your notes immediately turn this one into something special — keep reading. 👀)

4Putting "NOT" on things: Inverse & Contrapositive

🧸 ELI5

First, meet the negation: it's the exact opposite of a sentence, usually by sticking "not" in it.

"It is raining" → negation: "It is not raining." That's it. No fancier words — "I am overjoyed" is not the negation of "I am happy" (you could be neither!). The negation is boring on purpose: just add "not". 🪄

Now you can make two more family members of your promise:

  • Inverse = put "not" on both halves. (No swap!)
  • Contrapositive = put "not" on both halves AND swap. (The full combo!)
📝 Test-speak
NameRecipeFormula
Original (conditional)as writtenp → q
Converseswapq → p
Inversenegate both¬p → ¬q
Contrapositive "CP" in your notesswap and negate both¬q → ¬p

(¬ is the symbol for "not".)

The rain example from your notes — all four versions

Original: If it is not raining, then I am happy.

VersionSentenceWhat we did
Converse"If I am happy, then it is not raining."swapped
Inverse"If it is raining, then I am not happy."not'd both halves
Contrapositive"If I am not happy, then it is raining."not'd both + swapped
⚠️ Trap alert

Look at the inverse: "it is not raining" got negated into… "it is raining". Two NOTs cancel — like a double negative: "I don't have no homework" actually means you do have homework. When you negate a sentence that already has "not", the "not" disappears.

🧸 ELI5

Truth buddies. The original and its contrapositive are secretly the same fact, just told backwards-and-flipped:

"If it's a balloon, then it can float." ↔ "If it can't float, then it's not a balloon." Same information!

The converse and the inverse are also buddies: whenever one is true, the other is true. (But the converse/inverse pair can disagree with the original pair!)

Your notes said: "inverse and converse / converse and inverse" — this is that pattern: the pairs travel together.
✏️ Try it

For "If x = 5, then x² = 25" write the contrapositive and the inverse.

tap to reveal

Contrapositive: "If x² ≠ 25, then x ≠ 5." (swap + not both — and it's TRUE, buddy of the true original ✅)

Inverse: "If x ≠ 5, then x² ≠ 25." …but x = −5 breaks it! (−5 ≠ 5, yet (−5)² = 25.) So the inverse is FALSE here — proof that an inverse doesn't have to match its original. Only the contrapositive always matches. 🔑

5The Biconditional: when both directions work ("IFF")

🧸 ELI5

Sometimes a promise works both ways. Then you don't need two sentences — you smash them together with the magic words "if and only if" (short version: IFF). That super-sentence is called a biconditional statement.

It's like a two-way door 🚪↔️ — you can walk in from either side. But you only get the door if both directions are actually true!

📝 Test-speak

Biconditional: a statement written as p if and only if q (p ↔ q). It's allowed only when the conditional AND its converse are both true — exactly what your notes say: "If Converse and Conditional Statement true then Biconditional Statement."

Your notes' two examples

Collinear points 🎯

• Conditional: "If 3 points lie on the same line, then they are collinear." ✅
• Converse: "If 3 points are collinear, then they lie on the same line." ✅

→ Both true, so: "Three points are collinear if and only if they lie on the same line."

Betweenness + segment addition 📏

• "If B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC." ✅
• "If AB + BC = AC, then B is between A and C." ✅

→ "B is between A and C if and only if AB + BC = AC." (Your notes even drew the little diagram for this one.)

⚠️ Trap alert

Not every conditional earns a biconditional. "x = 5 → x² = 25" is true, but its converse fails (x = −5), so "x = 5 if and only if x² = 25" would be wrong. If the test asks "can this be written as a biconditional?", your job is: check the original ✅, check the converse 🔍, only then say yes.

✏️ Try it

Can you write a biconditional? "If a point is the midpoint of a segment, then it divides the segment into two equal parts."

tap to reveal
Check the converse: "If a point divides a segment into two equal parts, then it is the midpoint." ✅ True both ways! Biconditional: "A point is the midpoint of a segment if and only if it divides the segment into two equal parts." (Compare with the Midpoint Theorem in §8 — same idea!)

6Counterexamples: the promise-buster

🧸 ELI5

Someone says: "All swans are white." You don't need a research paper to prove them wrong — you need one black swan. 🦢

A counterexample is exactly that black swan: one example where the promise breaks, and the whole statement is dead. Your notes call it "the thing which disproves the given statement."

📝 Test-speak

To disprove if p, then q you need an example where p is true but q is false. (That's the only combo that counts as "breaking" the promise.)

Your notes' two examples — memorized on the spot

Murder suspect #1: "If x² = 49, then x = 7."

Counterexample: x = −7. Check the receipt: (−7)² = 49 ✅ (so p was true)… but −7 ≠ 7 ❌. Promise broken. 💀

Murder suspect #2: "If AB ≅ BC, then B is the midpoint of AC."

Counterexample from your notes: make a triangle-ish picture where AB and BC are the same length, but B doesn't even sit on segment AC. A midpoint has to actually BE on the segment — equal lengths elsewhere in space don't count!

AB ≅ BC… but B is nowhere near the middle of AC. Counterexample confirmed.
⚠️ Trap alert

Examples can never prove an "always" statement — only a proof does that. But one counterexample is enough to disprove it. Also: a "counterexample" that doesn't actually make p true is not a counterexample (no, x = 3 doesn't break "if x² = 49 then x = 7" — it doesn't even satisfy the setup).

✏️ Try it

Find a counterexample: "If x² = 25, then x = 5."

tap to reveal
x = −5: (−5)² = 25 ✅, but −5 ≠ 5 ❌. (Same trick as the x² = 49 one — see why the class keeps using it?)

7The math rules: Properties of Equality

🧸 ELI5

An equation is a balance scale ⚖️. The two sides are equally heavy. Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other — then it stays balanced. That's basically all these property names are about: allowed moves on a balanced scale.

📝 Test-speak
PropertyRulePlain meaning (ELI5)You'll see it as a reason for…
Reflexivea = a"A thing equals itself.""m∠2 = m∠2" — the classic line in angle proofs
Symmetricif a = b, then b = a"Same fact, read backwards."flipping an equation around
Transitiveif a = b and b = c, then a = c"Chain: if two things match a middle thing, they match each other."linking three equal quantities
Substitutionif a = b, replace a with b (or b with a) anywhere"Identical twins — swap them freely."replacing RS with PS, m∠1 with m∠3, etc.
Additionif a = b, then a + c = b + c"Add the same snack to both plates."adding ½x to both sides; adding two equal equations together
Subtractionif a = b, then a − c = b − c"Take the same thing off both sides."the finish line of several proofs (leftover parts equal)
Multiplicationif a = b, then a·c = b·c"Double both pans — still balanced."multiplying both sides by ½ / by 2
Divisionif a = b, then a ÷ c = b ÷ c (c ≠ 0)"Share both pans between the same friends."dividing both sides to isolate x
⚠️ Trap alert

On the test, name properties exactly — "Substitution Property of Equality", "Reflexive Property" — matching your teacher's wording from class. The #1 mix-up: Reflexive (a = a — a thing and itself) vs Substitution (swapping equal things). If the line says "m∠2 = m∠2", that's Reflexive, not Substitution!

✏️ Try it

Name the property each time:

  1. "If AB = CD and CD = EF, then AB = EF."
  2. "If m∠1 = m∠2, then m∠2 = m∠1."
  3. "ST = ST."
  4. "If m∠A = m∠B, then m∠A + 10 = m∠B + 10."
tap to reveal
  1. Transitive (three things, chained)
  2. Symmetric (read backwards)
  3. Reflexive (a thing equals itself)
  4. Addition Property of Equality (same thing added to both sides)

8Segments & angles: the two postulates + two theorems

🧸 ELI5

Time to leave Sentence World and enter Picture World. Four tools power every proof in your notes:

  • Segment Addition — a broken stick: the pieces add up to the whole stick.
  • Angle Addition — a sliced pizza: the slices add up to the whole slice stack.
  • Midpoint — the fair ruler cut: exactly in the middle.
  • Angle Bisector — the fair pizza cut: straight down the middle of the angle.

1) Segment Addition Postulate

📝 Test-speak

If B is between A and C, then AB + BC = AC. (And per your notes, both directions work — a bonus biconditional: "B is between A and C iff AB + BC = AC.")

Going right? Add the pieces. Given the whole and one piece? Subtract.

2) Angle Addition Postulate

📝 Test-speak

If ray OB sits inside ∠AOC (between OA and OC), then m∠AOB + m∠BOC = m∠AOC. (In your proofs: "m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠WOY" style lines — that's this postulate working.)

3) Midpoint — the fair ruler cut

📝 Test-speak

Definition of midpoint: if M is the midpoint of AB, then AM ≅ MB and AM = MB.

Midpoint Theorem (boxed in your notes): if M is the midpoint of AB, then AM = ½ AB and MB = ½ AB.

🔍 Little detail that wins points

Notice your notes write AM ≅ MB AND AM = MB. ≅ is for segments ("these two segments are congruent — same size"); = is for numbers ("the lengths are equal"). You can do arithmetic on numbers ("AM = ½AB"), not on segments. Little symbol, big points. ✍️

4) Angle Bisector — the fair pizza cut

📝 Test-speak

Definition of angle bisector: if a ray bisects an angle, then it splits it into two equal angles.

Angle Bisector Theorem (boxed in your notes): if ray OT bisects ∠AOB, then m∠AOT = ½ m∠AOB and m∠TOB = ½ m∠AOB (so the two halves are equal to each other, too).

✏️ Try it

M is the midpoint of AB. If AM = 3x + 2 and MB = 5x − 10, find x and AB.

tap to reveal

Midpoint means the halves are equal → set them equal: 3x + 2 = 5x − 10.

Add 10: 3x + 12 = 5x → subtract 3x: 12 = 2x → x = 6.

Then AM = 3(6) + 2 = 20, MB = 5(6) − 10 = 20 ✅ → AB = 40.

9Two-column proofs: the recipe (+ every proof from your notes, solved)

🧸 ELI5

A proof is a receipt. 🧾 Every line is: what I claim + why I'm allowed to claim it.

Left column = Statements (the claims). Right column = Reasons (the permission slips). First line: the Given (free clue, no permission needed). Last line: what you were asked to prove. Every line in between must be earned with a reason from the menu below — no skipping steps, no "trust me bro."

📝 Test-speak

The Golden Menu of Reasons — when the test says "state the reason", it's one of these:

FamilyMembers
Giventhe info the problem hands you (free!)
DefinitionsDefinition of midpoint · Definition of angle bisector · Definition of congruence
PostulatesSegment Addition Postulate · Angle Addition Postulate
PropertiesReflexive · Symmetric · Transitive · Substitution · Addition · Subtraction · Multiplication · Division (of Equality)
TheoremsMidpoint Theorem · Angle Bisector Theorem

Format: two columns, Statements | Reasons, numbered lines, first = Given, last = Prove. ✔️

🛠️ How to attack ANY proof on Thursday
  1. Copy the Given as line 1 — and re-draw/label the figure with tick marks and angle numbers.
  2. Write what you must prove as your personal finish line (don't put it in the table yet!).
  3. Ask: "What pieces add up to the whole?" → that's usually a Segment/Angle Addition move.
  4. Ask: "Which two things are equal, and can I swap one in?" → Substitution.
  5. Ask: "Is something equal to itself, or can I add/subtract the same thing on both sides?" → Reflexive / Addition / Subtraction.
  6. Write the finish line last. Done — that's a proof.

Proof 1 — the X of segments (your p.4)

Given: RS = PS and ST = SQ  ·  Prove: RT = PQ

Story version: two sticks (RT and PQ) cross at S, and the matching pieces are equal (the tick marks!). If the pieces match in pairs, the whole sticks must match.

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. RS = PS, ST = SQ1. Given
2. RS + ST = RT  ·  PS + SQ = PQ2. Segment Addition Postulate
3. RT = PQ3. Substitution Property

Why step 3 works: since RS = PS and ST = SQ, the sum RS + ST equals the sum PS + SQ. But those sums are RT and PQ. Match! 🎯

Proof 2 — algebra in disguise (your p.4)

Given: 3x = 6 − ½x  ·  Prove: x = 12⁄7

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. 3x = 6 − ½x1. Given
2. 3½x = 62. Addition Property of Equality (add ½x to both sides)
3. x = 12⁄73. Division (Multiplication) Property of Equality (divide both sides by 3½)

The arithmetic: 3x + ½x = 3½x. Then x = 6 ÷ 3½ = 6 ÷ (7/2) = 6 × (2/7) = 12/7. Same answer as the bottom of your notes. ✅

Proof 3 — equal big angles → equal small angles (your p.5)

Given: m∠AOC = m∠BOD  ·  Prove: m∠1 = m∠3

Figure: four rays A, B, C, D fan out from O. ∠1 = between A and B; ∠2 = between B and C; ∠3 = between C and D.

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. m∠AOC = m∠BOD1. Given
2. m∠AOC = m∠1 + m∠2  ·  m∠BOD = m∠2 + m∠32. Angle Addition Postulate
3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠2 + m∠33. Substitution Property
4. m∠2 = m∠24. Reflexive Property
5. m∠1 = m∠35. Subtraction Property of Equality

Story: both big angles contain the same middle slice (∠2). Big = Big → cut the same slice off both → leftovers equal. Step 4 (m∠2 = m∠2) is the "of course!" line that earns the right to subtract. 🍰

Proof 4 — equal small angles → equal big angles (your p.7) — the reverse trick!

Given: m∠1 = m∠3  ·  Prove: m∠WOY = m∠ZOX

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. m∠1 = m∠31. Given
2. m∠2 = m∠22. Reflexive Property
3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠3 + m∠23. Addition Property of Equality
4. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠WOY  ·  m∠2 + m∠3 = m∠ZOX4. Angle Addition Postulate
5. m∠WOY = m∠ZOX5. Substitution Property

Proof 3 cut the same slice off both sides; Proof 4 glues the same slice ON to both sides. Same family, opposite direction. Students who memorize the pair never get stuck. 🔁

Proof 5 — bisectors of equal angles (your p.9)

Given: SV bisects ∠RST, RV bisects ∠SRT, and m∠RST = m∠SRT  ·  Prove: m∠1 = m∠2

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. SV bisects ∠RST  ·  RV bisects ∠SRT1. Given
2. m∠1 = ½ m∠RST  ·  m∠2 = ½ m∠SRT2. Angle Bisector Theorem
3. m∠RST = m∠SRT3. Given
4. ½ m∠RST = ½ m∠SRT4. Multiplication Property of Equality
5. m∠1 = m∠25. Substitution Property

Story: two angles are the same size. You cut each one exactly in half. Halves of equal things are equal — that's the whole proof. ✂️

Proof 6 — equal wholes, equal parts → equal leftovers (your p.6)

Given: ST = RN and IT = RV  ·  Prove: SI = VN

Two-column proof
StatementsReasons
1. ST = RN1. Given
2. ST = SI + IT  ·  RN = RV + VN2. Segment Addition Postulate
3. SI + IT = RV + VN3. Substitution Property
4. IT = RV4. Given
5. SI = VN5. Subtraction Property of Equality

Story: two whole segments are equal, and each has an equal little piece marked off. Cut off the matching piece from both → the leftover parts are equal. (Handwriting note: a couple of these letters are hard to read on the photo — the method is what matters and it's the same Proof-1 idea, just with subtraction at the end.) ✂️

10Cheat sheet — the one-page brain dump

The four versions of a promise

original p → q

If it is not raining, then I am happy.

the promise as written

converse q → p

If I am happy, then it is not raining.

SWAP the halves

inverse ¬p → ¬q

If it is raining, then I am not happy.

NOT on both (double-not cancels!)

contrapositive ¬q → ¬p

If I am not happy, then it is raining.

SWAP + NOT both · same truth as original ⭐

Truth buddies: original ⭐ contrapositive (always same truth) · converse ⭐ inverse (always same truth).
Biconditional (p ↔ q, "p if and only if q") only when original AND converse are both true.
Counterexample = one example with p true, q false → kills the statement. One is enough. ☠️

Properties of equality

  • Reflexive: a = a
  • Symmetric: a = b → b = a
  • Transitive: a = b, b = c → a = c
  • Substitution: swap a ↔ b anywhere
  • Addition: a = b → a + c = b + c
  • Subtraction: a = b → a − c = b − c
  • Multiplication: a = b → ac = bc
  • Division: a = b → a/c = b/c (c ≠ 0)

Postulates & Theorems

  • Segment Addition: B between A & C → AB + BC = AC (works both ways!)
  • Angle Addition: inner ray → m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠big
  • Midpoint Theorem: M midpoint → AM = MB = ½AB
  • Angle Bisector Theorem: ray splits → each half = ½ whole
  • Def. of midpoint: → AM ≅ MB (and AM = MB)
  • Def. of angle bisector: → the two angles are equal

Symbols & phrases

p → q  ·  q → p  ·  ¬p → ¬q  ·  ¬q → ¬p  ·  p ↔ q  ·  ∠  ·  m∠  ·  ≅ (congruent)  ·  = (equal measure)  ·  ½

"blw" in your notes = between. "CP" = contrapositive. Sentence shufflers: if p then q = p implies q = p only if q = q if p. In "p only if q", the q is the conclusion — trap! 🪤

11Your 48-hour plan (test is Thursday)

🌙 Tuesday night (tonight)

  • Read this guide start to finish — ~35 min. Do the ✏️ Try-it reveals as you go.
  • Flashcards.html once through — 10 min. Don't grind; just meet the terms.
  • Close the laptop. Sleep is a study tool. 😴

📅 Wednesday

  • Practice-Test.html, one full sitting — ~45 min, timer on if you can.
  • Go through every miss and read the explanation. Missed a section? Re-read that guide section once.
  • Flashcards again before bed — you'll be shocked how much sticks the second time.

☀️ Thursday morning

  • Skim §10 Cheat sheet + the Truth-buddies diagram (§4) + quick-fire table (§9).
  • 10 minutes, max. You prepared — now just remind, don't cram.

🎯 Test-day moves

  • Rewrite weird sentences as If …, then … before labeling anything.
  • Underline WHICH version they ask for (converse? inverse? contrapositive?) — the #1 lost-points mistake.
  • Proofs: Given first, prove-line last, every line gets a reason.
  • Numeric answers: plug back in to check (x = 12/7 works — try it).

If 3 pts lie on the same line then they are collinear points.
▸ Converse: If 3 pts are collinear then they lie on same line.

If Converse and Conditional Statement are true → Biconditional Statement
   [IFF boxed] = if and only if

Eg: If B is blw ("between") A and C then AB + BC = AC.
▸ Converse: If AB + BC = AC then B is blw A and C.  → Biconditional Statement

Counterexample: which disproves the Given Statement.
Eg: "If AB ≅ BC then B is midpoint of AC" — killed by a figure where B is NOT on AC.

Inverse:        If ¬P then ¬Q     (notes: "If NP then NQ")
Contrapositive: If ¬Q then ¬P     (notes: "If NQ then NP")
Note: inverse and converse / converse and inverse [travel together]

If x² = 49 then x = 7.           Counterexample: x = −7

Given: If it is not raining then I am happy.
   a. I am not happy      b. It is not raining
   c. I am overjoyed      d. It is raining

Converse:        If I am happy then it is not raining.
Inverse:         If it is raining then I am not happy.
CP (contrapositive): If I am not happy then it is raining.

Page 4 — Properties of equality + two full proofs (segment X + algebra)

cleaned transcription 
Given: RT and PQ intersect at S so that RS = PS and ST = SQ.  Prove: RT = PQ.

Properties:
• Substitution: If a = b, then you can substitute a for b or b for a.
• Symmetric:  If a = b then b = a.
• Reflexive:  a = a.
• Transitive: If a = b, b = c then a = c.

Proof 1
  1. RS = PS, ST = SQ                     | Given
  2. RS + ST = RT  ·  PS + SQ = PQ        | Addition Prop of Equality / Segment Addition Post
  3. RT = PQ                              | Substitution Prop

Proof 2  (solve 3x = 6 − ½x)
  1. 3x = 6 − ½x        | Given
  2. 3½x = 6            | Addition Prop of Equality   (margin: + ½x both sides)
  3. x = 12/7           | Multiplication Prop of Equality   (÷ 3½ both sides)
  Conclusion: x = 12/7

Page 5 — Angle proof: equal big angles → equal small angles

cleaned transcription 
Given: m∠AOC = m∠BOD  [? best-read]   To prove: m∠1 = m∠3
Figure: four rays from O labeled A, B, C, D; angles 1, 2, 3 between them.

  1. m∠AOC = m∠BOD                | Given
  2. m∠AOC = m∠1 + m∠2            | Angle Addition Post
     m∠BOD = m∠2 + m∠3            |
  3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠2 + m∠3        | Substitution Prop
  4. m∠2 = m∠2                    | Reflexive Prop
  5. m∠1 = m∠3                    | Subtraction Prop

Page 6 — Segment proof: equal wholes + equal parts → equal leftovers

cleaned transcription 
Given: ST = RN, IT = RV  [? a few letters hard to read — see guide note]   To prove: SI = VN

Plan:  ST = SI + IT  ·  RN = RV + VN  ·  SI + IT = RV + VN  →  SI = VN

  1. ST = RN                        | Given
  2. ST = SI + IT  ·  RN = RV + VN  | Segment Addition Post
  3. SI + IT = RV + VN              | Substitution Prop
  4. IT = RV                        | Given
  5. SI = VN                        | Subtraction Prop

Page 7 — Reverse angle proof + Midpoint Theorem

cleaned transcription 
Given: m∠1 = m∠3.   To prove: m∠WOY = m∠ZOX
Plan: ∠1 = ∠3 · WOY = ∠1 + ∠2 · ZOX = ∠2 + ∠3 → prove equal.

  1. m∠1 = m∠3                     | Given
  2. m∠2 = m∠2                     | Reflexive Prop
  3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠3 + m∠2         | Addition Prop of Equality
  4. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠WOY             | Angle Addition Post
     m∠2 + m∠3 = m∠ZOX             |
  5. m∠WOY = m∠ZOX                 | Substitution Prop

Midpoint Theorem [boxed]:
  If M is the midpoint of AB then AM = ½ AB, MB = ½ AB.
  [circled:] AM ≅ MB,  AM = MB

Page 8 — Angle Bisector Theorem + the quick-fire theorem list

cleaned transcription 
Angle Bisector Theorem [boxed]:
  If OT bisects ∠AOB:  m∠AOT = ½ m∠AOB  ·  m∠TOB = ½ m∠AOB

Quick-fire list:
  1. If GK is the bisector of ∠FGJ, then m∠3 = ½ m∠FGJ     → Angle bisector theorem
  2. FK + KJ = FJ                                          → Segment Addition Post
  3. m∠1 + m∠2 = m∠FKJ                                     → Angle Addition Post
  4. If K is the midpoint of FJ, then FK = ½ FJ            → Midpoint theorem

Figure: "bowtie" of two triangles sharing G (points F, G, H, K, J, I) with tick marks.

Given: SV bisects ∠RST · RV bisects ∠SRT · m∠RST = m∠SRT.   To prove: m∠1 = m∠2
Also written: m∠1 = ½ m∠RST  ·  m∠2 = ½ m∠SRT

  1. SV bisects ∠RST (RV bisects ∠SRT)  | Given
  2. m∠1 = ½ m∠RST  ·  m∠2 = ½ m∠SRT    | Angle Bisector Theorem
  3. m∠RST = m∠SRT                      | Given
  4. ½ m∠RST = ½ m∠SRT                  | Multiplication Prop of Equality
  5. m∠1 = m∠2                          | Substitution Prop
